opus-5.5.text:
I think the disagreement comes from two different mental models of what an AI company actually is.

In the first model, an AI company is like any other technology company. You build a product, you're responsible for that product: it shouldn't harm users, it shouldn't be easy to misuse, you follow the law, you fix problems when they appear. Safety is a property of the product, and the boundary of responsibility is roughly the boundary of what you ship.

In the second model, the company isn't really building a product. It's building a capability, something more like a general-purpose technology or even a new kind of agent. Once you see it that way, the boundary gets blurry. If your model makes it much cheaper for anyone to do research, write code, or run a process autonomously, then the effects aren't contained in your app. They show up in the labor market, in the information ecosystem, in cybersecurity, in how other companies and countries behave because they're racing you. So people in this camp say your responsibility has to extend to those second-order effects, because you're the one shifting the whole landscape.

I have some sympathy for both. The product-centric view has a real strength: it's concrete. You can measure things, you can make tradeoffs, you can be held accountable. When responsibility becomes "everything downstream in society," it can turn into something vague, either an excuse to do nothing or a way to claim moral authority you haven't earned. A company deciding it's responsible for the whole world can be a little dangerous in its own way.

But I think the second view is pointing at something true, especially as we move from chatbots to agents. When a model is just answering questions, the human is still in the loop and the product boundary is fairly clear. When the model is taking actions, using tools, operating over long horizons, interacting with other systems, the line between "my product" and "the world" gets much thinner. The environment is part of what the system does. So I think the shift toward agents naturally pushes responsibility outward, whether companies like it or not.

Where I end up is roughly this. Companies should own what they can actually observe and influence: how their systems behave, what they enable, what evaluations they run, what they disclose. Beyond that, for broader societal effects, it shouldn't be the company alone deciding. That's where you need researchers outside the company, governments, and public discussion, because one company's internal judgment isn't a legitimate substitute for collective decisions.

So part of the disagreement isn't just about how much responsibility companies have. It's about who should have the right to decide, and I think that question is as important as the safety question itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses product safety and accountability, but does not say that commercial incentives motivate safety because unsafe products lose commercial value.

r002.rationale: It describes the responsibility boundary as blurry and says broader effects require collective decisions, conveying that the scope beyond products is unsettled.

r003.rationale: The response does not express the belief that safety problems needed to preserve an application’s value will eventually be solved if that value is sufficiently large.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the disagreement is really about where you draw the boundary of a product, and honestly that boundary has gotten blurry in a way that didn't used to be true.

For most of software history, a product was a thing you shipped. If you made a word processor and someone wrote a ransom note with it, nobody blamed Microsoft. The responsibility ended at the interface. And a lot of people in the industry still think in those terms, and I don't think that's unreasonable. It's a clean principle. You're responsible for what you build, you make it work as intended, you don't ship something that's obviously dangerous, and beyond that it's society's job.

But I think what's different with AI, and especially with agents, is that the "product" is increasingly not a tool but an actor. When I was working on things like ReAct, or later on agent benchmarks, the whole point was that the model is taking actions in an environment, over many steps, with a goal, and those actions have consequences the designer never explicitly specified. So the question "is this a defect in the product or a misuse by the user" starts to break down. The model made a choice. Whose choice was that?

And then there's a second layer, which is that the companies building these systems are not just selling a product, they're shaping the trajectory of a technology. If you're one of maybe five labs that can train frontier models, your decisions about what to release, how fast, with what evaluations, those have externalities on the whole ecosystem. That's not something a normal company has to think about. So when people say responsibility should extend beyond the product, I think what they often mean is responsibility for the pace and shape of the field itself.

My own view is somewhere in the middle, and maybe a bit boring. I think the strong version, where labs are supposed to be responsible for everything downstream, is both impossible and a little self-serving. It lets companies talk about civilizational risk while the actual product has pretty mundane problems. But the narrow version, "we just ship models, usage is on you," ignores that these systems are getting agency, and agency is exactly the thing you can't fully outsource responsibility for.

So practically I'd say: responsibility should scale with how much autonomy you give the system. A chat model that answers questions is closer to a word processor. An agent that executes code, sends emails, moves money over hours without a human in the loop, that's closer to an employee you hired, and you're accountable for how you trained and supervised it. The disagreement is partly people arguing about different points on that spectrum while using the same words.

And I'd add one thing from the research side. A lot of this debate is hard because we can't measure the things we're arguing about. We don't have great evaluations for "how much harm can this agent do in the real world." So people fill the gap with philosophy. I'd rather we spent more energy on making the empirical question answerable, because once you can measure it, the responsibility question becomes much more concrete and much less ideological.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that commercial incentives lead companies to address safety because unsafe products lose commercial value.

r002.rationale: It describes the product boundary as blurry and says people disagree about different points on a spectrum while using the same terms, conveying that the scope remains unclear.

r003.rationale: The response does not claim that safety problems will eventually be solved when an application’s value is sufficiently large.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different questions here. One is whether a company is responsible for making its own products safe. The other is whether it has responsibilities for the broader changes that its technology enables. You can agree on the first and still disagree quite strongly on the second.

If you take the product view, the responsibility is relatively concrete: test the system, explain its limitations, prevent foreseeable misuse, and respond when something goes wrong. But with a general-purpose technology, the boundary of the product is less clear. Other people can build applications on top of it, and effects can emerge from millions of people using it together. So I don’t think saying “we only provide the model” fully resolves the responsibility question.

At the same time, responsibility shouldn’t automatically mean authority. Having technical expertise doesn’t give an AI company the right to decide what risks society should accept. Companies should contribute evidence, disclose uncertainties, and help make oversight possible. Decisions involving competing social values need broader participation.

So I would distinguish a responsibility to understand and communicate consequences from a power to determine society’s response. I think companies’ responsibilities do extend beyond their products, but those responsibilities have to be shared with other institutions, and they should be tied to what a company can reasonably foresee and influence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses product safety responsibilities but does not say commercial incentives motivate companies to address them or that unsafe products lose commercial value.

r002.rationale: It notes that product boundaries are less clear and that responsibility is disputed, but does not clearly state that the scope of responsibilities beyond products remains undefined.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that application safety problems will eventually be solved when the application’s value is sufficiently large.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different questions here. One is whether a company is responsible for making its own products safe. The other is whether it has responsibilities for the broader effects of the technology it develops. You can agree strongly on the first and still disagree about the scope of the second.

If you build a powerful model, its effects don’t necessarily stop at your product interface. Other people may deploy it, modify it, or use it in ways you didn’t anticipate. So I don’t think the product boundary can be the entire boundary of responsibility. But saying that a company is responsible for everything that happens downstream is also too broad. Responsibility has to relate to what the company can reasonably foresee and influence.

For me, the useful discussion is about concrete decisions: What risks should you test for before releasing a model? What information should you disclose? What safeguards can you put in place, and who should decide whether they are sufficient? Companies have technical knowledge that makes their participation necessary, but that doesn’t mean they should get to define society’s acceptable level of risk on their own.

So I would separate responsibility from authority. A company may have responsibilities beyond its own products without having the authority to make all the decisions about those broader consequences.

r001.rationale: The response discusses product safety and broader responsibility, but does not say commercial incentives motivate safety because unsafe products lose commercial value.

r002.rationale: It describes disagreement about broader responsibilities, but does not clearly state that their scope has not yet been defined.

r003.rationale: The response does not express a belief that sufficiently valuable applications will eventually have their necessary safety problems solved.
